opus-5.5.text:
That's probably the most common objection we heard, and honestly, it was our own first instinct too. The conventional wisdom in latent diffusion has been that you want to compress as aggressively as possible: take the image, squeeze it into a very low-dimensional latent, maybe four or sixteen channels, because a smaller space should be easier for the diffusion model to learn. Representation encoders like DINO or SigLIP give you something like 768 or more channels per token, so people assumed diffusion in that space would just fall apart.

What we found is that "high-dimensional" isn't really the problem. The problem is whether your model and your training recipe actually respect that dimensionality. When we first tried a standard DiT on these representation latents, it didn't work well, and it would have been easy to conclude "see, high dimension is bad." But when we dug in, there were some fairly concrete reasons.

First, model width. If the transformer's hidden width is smaller than the token dimension, the model basically can't fit the data, even on a single image. Once the width matches or exceeds the latent dimension, it suddenly works. So it's a capacity question, not a fundamental barrier.

Second, the noise schedule. In higher dimensions, the same noise level actually destroys much less information, so you need to shift the schedule according to dimensionality, similar to what people already do when going to higher resolutions. Once you account for that, training becomes much more stable.

Third, the decoder. Diffusion outputs are never perfectly on the data manifold, so we train the decoder with some noise augmentation so it's robust to slightly off-distribution latents.

And once you handle those things, the high-dimensional space turns out to be an advantage. These representations are semantically very structured. The model doesn't spend its capacity figuring out what an object is from scratch; that's already organized in the space. So you get faster convergence and better generation quality, not worse.

The broader point I'd make is that a lot of what we think of as "hard" in deep learning is really "hard under our current defaults." Low-dimensional VAE latents became the default partly by historical accident, because that's what made things work at the time. It doesn't mean it's the right abstraction forever. I think there's a real opportunity for generation and understanding to share the same representation space, and you only get there if you're willing to question that compression assumption.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a very natural concern, and honestly it's the first thing people bring up when I talk about this work. The intuition goes: if a VAE compresses an image down to a 4- or 16-channel latent, the diffusion model only has to fit a small, smooth space. If you instead ask it to generate in a representation that's hundreds or thousands of dimensions, say the feature space of a self-supervised encoder like DINO, surely you've made the problem much harder. More dimensions, more to model.

But I think this conflates dimensionality with difficulty. What matters is not how many numbers you're predicting, it's how structured those numbers are. Pixel space is also high-dimensional, and it's hard, but not because of the count. It's hard because the information is spread out in a way that has very little semantic organization. Most of the variance is in high-frequency detail that doesn't matter for the content of the image. A good semantic representation is the opposite. It's high-dimensional on paper, but the data lives on a much lower-dimensional, better-behaved manifold inside that space. Nearby points mean similar things. Directions have meaning. That's exactly the kind of space a generative model wants.

The empirical evidence lines up with this. In our REPA work, just aligning diffusion transformer features to a pretrained encoder's representation sped up training by something like 17x. The model wasn't being asked to do more; it was being told where the useful structure already is. When you take that further and actually generate in the representation space, you see the same thing. Convergence gets faster, not slower, even though the nominal dimension is higher.

There's a flip side I'll admit. Learning in that space is easier, but you've pushed a different problem elsewhere: you now need a decoder that can turn a semantic representation back into pixels, and that representation may have thrown away details you want to recover. So the real design question isn't "high-dimensional versus low-dimensional." It's which information you want the generative model to spend its capacity on, and which you're comfortable delegating to a decoder. I'd rather have the hard generative model work on semantics and let a lightweight component fill in texture, than the other way around, which is honestly what we've been doing with pixel-oriented VAE latents.

So I don't dismiss the concern, but I think the burden of proof has shifted. Compression was a good trick when we didn't have strong representations. Now we do, and I think the field should stop treating the latent space as a given and start treating it as a design choice.

r001.rationale: It says generating in the higher-dimensional representation converges faster, directly countering the concern that the larger dimension makes learning harder.

r002.rationale: It discusses semantic structure and details that may be lost, but does not state that higher-dimensional representations contain information absent from lower-dimensional ones.

r003.rationale: It describes a better-behaved manifold and meaningful directions, but does not explain that lifting data into higher dimensions can make it linearly separable.

astra-6.text:
I think that concern is reasonable, but we should distinguish dimensionality from complexity. A representation can be high-dimensional and still have a structure that makes learning easier. Conversely, a compact representation can be difficult to model if it entangles a lot of information.

So the question is really: what does that representation expose to the model? If it organizes the meaningful factors of an image well, the additional dimensions may actually help. You’re giving the model useful structure rather than asking it to discover everything from scratch.

Of course, higher dimensionality can increase computation, and you may need to adapt the architecture or training setup. But that’s different from saying the learning problem is inherently harder. I would treat that as an empirical question: with an appropriate model, does the representation make generation easier or harder?

sol-6.1.text:
I think that concern is reasonable, but dimensionality alone doesn’t tell you how difficult a representation is to learn. You also have to ask how the information is organized. A lower-dimensional representation can be very compressed and entangled, while a higher-dimensional representation can expose structure that makes learning easier.

For image generation, the question is whether the model has to learn arbitrary variation in all those dimensions, or whether the representations occupy a structured manifold. If there’s strong structure, the effective problem can be much simpler than the raw dimensionality suggests.

That doesn’t mean you can ignore the challenge. The architecture and the training objective have to be suited to that representation. But I wouldn’t conclude that a representation is harder to model simply because it has more dimensions. I’d look at what information it preserves, how accessible that information is, and whether the generative model can use it effectively.
